I'll make the case why you should buy a business and use AI agents to 3x EBITDA. By the end of this dead simple guide, you'll know how to find the right business, buy it, and run it with agents, down to the folders and prompts. It's kinda long (~10-15 min read) but for those interested, worth it.
~$5 trillion worth of American businesses will change hands by 2035, according to McKinsey. Most belong to baby boomers heading into retirement, and a lot of those owners have nobody lined up to buy them.
In Bellingham, Washington, there's an accounting firm called Larson Gross. It was founded in 1949. It has five offices and about 200 employees, and Thrive Holdings recently bought a stake in it.
This tax season, the firm's AI processed 7,000 returns. Accountants saved 31% of their time on average. One accountant took a job that used to eat 180 hour
hits.draft_en:
The boring business next door is about to get an AI operating system.

Not a chatbot bolted on. Agents that eat 30% of the hours on work that already has customers, licenses, and trust.

McKinsey-sized wealth transfer is coming as boomers exit. The edge is not inventing a new SaaS. It is buying cashflow and rewriting the work folder with agents.

If you can underwrite a service firm and ship an agent stack, you are not competing with OpenAI. You are competing with owners who still bill by the hour.

Pick one vertical. Map the 5 jobs that burn time. Automate those first. Then raise on EBITDA, not vibes.
hits.video_tip: 12–18s: cold open on a dusty storefront → cut to agent dashboard chewing tax returns / tickets → end card “buy cashflow, rent intelligence.”

hits.draft_en:
Claude Code is cool again. Six months ago people sworn off it. That is the tell.

AI tooling fashion flips faster than frameworks. The winners are not the ones married to last quarter’s stack. They are the ones who keep a 48-hour retool muscle.

I am not loyal to a model. I am loyal to shipping. When the cool tool moves, I move the workflow, keep the repo, keep the distribution.

If your identity is “I only use X,” you will get smoked by someone who switched on Tuesday.

Audit your stack weekly. Kill sacred cows. Ride the meta.
hits.video_tip: 8–12s flip-card montage: Cursor → Claude Code → Codex logos with timestamps, hard cut to terminal `git push`.

While the timeline argues about model scoreboards, coding agents shipped bot mode, local mode, and better subagents in the quiet.

That gap is the opportunity. Coverage lags product. If you wait for the thinkpiece, the early users already compounded.

My rule: every week, open one agent repo that is not trending yet. Run the changelog. Steal one workflow. Post the result.

The meta is not “which model is #1.” The meta is who operationalizes agents before the discourse catches up.

Ship the boring integration. Post the before/after. Let the discourse arrive late.
hits.video_tip: 10–15s screen record: agent changelog → bot mode toggle → local AI mode → split-screen “timeline debate” vs “you shipping.”

hits.name: Pieter Levels
hits.draft_en:
OpenAI “tens of thousands of incidents” is not a ghost story. It is a ops billboard.

When labs investigate at that volume, builders should assume two things: distribution is getting harder to fake, and agent autonomy will get throttled in production paths.

If your product depends on unbounded agent loops in someone else’s sandbox, you need a fallback: local models, tighter tools, human gates.

Fear posts print views. Durable products print when you design for the clampdown.

Assume rate limits, audits, and kill switches. Build anyway.
hits.video_tip: 9–12s: redacted “incident” counter spinning → hard cut to local model running offline → caption “design for the clampdown.”

While the timeline argues about model scoreboards, coding agents shipped bot mode, local mode, and better subagents in the quiet.

That gap is the opportunity. Coverage lags product. If you wait for the thinkpiece, the early users already compounded.

My rule: every week, open one agent repo that is not trending yet. Run the changelog. Steal one workflow. Post the result.

The meta is not “which model is #1.” The meta is who operationalizes agents before the discourse catches up.

Ship the boring integration. Post the before/after. Let the discourse arrive late.
drafts.video_tip: 10–15s screen record: agent changelog → bot mode toggle → local AI mode → split-screen “timeline debate” vs “you shipping.”

drafts.draft_en:
OpenAI “tens of thousands of incidents” is not a ghost story. It is a ops billboard.

When labs investigate at that volume, builders should assume two things: distribution is getting harder to fake, and agent autonomy will get throttled in production paths.

If your product depends on unbounded agent loops in someone else’s sandbox, you need a fallback: local models, tighter tools, human gates.

Fear posts print views. Durable products print when you design for the clampdown.

Assume rate limits, audits, and kill switches. Build anyway.
drafts.video_tip: 9–12s: redacted “incident” counter spinning → hard cut to local model running offline → caption “design for the clampdown.”
